# Humaneness Voice Small — S3 long-reference Rank-128 LoRA

This is a **semantic-backbone LoRA adapter**, not a standalone TTS model. Load
it on **[laion/Humaneness-Voice-Small](https://huggingface.co/laion/Humaneness-Voice-Small),
checkpoint `S3` (step 32,337)**. It was trained to condition on a distinct
speaker reference recording up to **187 MOSS-v2 frames = 14.96 seconds**. The
adapter is Rank 128, alpha 128 on `q_proj`, `k_proj`, `v_proj`, and `o_proj`
in all 28 Qwen3 semantic layers: 112 wrapped linears, 36,700,160 learned
parameters. The local MOSS-style Talker, 12-codebook audio heads and codec
were not tuned in this LoRA run. The base repo contains the complete roughly
715M-parameter model weights and architecture; the separate
[MOSS Audio Tokenizer v2](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer-v2)
encodes references and decodes generated codec tokens.

The original base S1–S10 *training loader* cropped references at 37 frames
(2.96 seconds). That was a data-loader choice, not a model context limit.
The first public base `code/infer.py` also **rejected references longer than
37 frames**; this was a real inference-code restriction, not just a stale
README claim. On 8 October 2026 we corrected the public base inference
example and documentation to accept a configurable reference ceiling. This
adapter's `code/infer.py` independently truncates at 187 frames, reports the
**actual** number of frames used, warns below about five seconds and never
silently applies the old 37-frame crop. Passing a 15-second WAV is not a
guarantee of better cloning; the full-panel comparison below does not
establish that.

## Files

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `adapter_model.pt` | Adapter-only weights, safe to load with `torch.load(..., weights_only=True)`. Contains a format ID, base identity, rank/alpha and 224 `a/b` tensors. |
| `resume_checkpoint.pt` | Original step-26,774 training checkpoint with the adapter **and complete AdamW optimizer state**, schedule position and provenance hashes. Use only from a trusted source; PyTorch optimizer objects require `weights_only=False`. |
| `code/infer.py`, `code/lora_layers.py` | Reference-aware inference, exact LoRA module and loader. |
| `training/` | Historical JUPITER worklist, prompt, QA, Slurm and LoRA training/evaluation source. These paths point to the original Reformo Scratch layout; regenerate the packed Parquet worklist and local assets for another machine or dataset. |
| `evaluation_summary.json` | Aggregate paired validation diagnostic. No audio or evaluation UIDs are published here. |
| `LICENSE` | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. |

## Inference

Use a CUDA environment with PyTorch, Transformers, NumPy, SoundFile,
Torchaudio and `huggingface_hub`. The codec is fetched from its upstream
repository. On JUPITER compute nodes without Internet access, pre-download
both the base model and codec into a compute-visible cache and pass
`--base-dir` to the script. The script downloads the base `S3` files when
`--base-dir` is omitted.

```bash
python code/infer.py \
  --base-dir /path/to/Humaneness-Voice-Small \
  --reference-wav /path/to/clean-other-utterance.wav \
  --language en --frames 90 --seed 777 \
  --prompt '(quietly, warmly) [3.2 seconds duration] Welcome back. I am glad you made it.' \
  --text 'Welcome back. I am glad you made it.' \
  --output welcome.wav
```

Use **another utterance from the intended speaker**, not the target
recording itself. Prefer a clean five-to-fifteen-second clip. `--frames` is
the *generation budget* at 12.5 semantic frames per second; it is not a
reference-length limit and not a promise of exact output duration. For a
caption prompt, put the caption and exact quoted text into `--prompt` and
the same literal spoken words into `--text`, for example
`CAPTION: gently amused, close conversational voice\nTRANSCRIPT: "Welcome back."`.
For historical `GENERAL:`/`SCRIPT:` prompting, pass both sections in
`--prompt`; script-only prompts contain the sentence-local parenthesized
performance cues without a `GENERAL:` block. The LoRA was trained with a
reference on **every** example, so no-reference inference is not supported
by this adapter script.

The public script first loads the exact S3 base state, ties its audio
embedding/output weights, attaches FP32 Rank-128 LoRA matrices, validates
all 224 parameter names, encodes the supplied reference with all **12**
MOSS-v2 codebooks, truncates it to at most 187 complete 80-ms frames,
and only then packs the dedicated reference channel. It prints
`reference_frames` and `reference_seconds` after generation. This makes an
accidental 37-frame crop visible in logs.

## Training provenance and continuation

The run started from the same published S3 step-32,337 base as the comparison
below, not from a previous adapter. It used one presentation per accepted
reference-eligible S3 UID from the original long-reference worklist, with
a distinct reference for every target. The worklist had 3,707,948 eligible
unique targets (8,832.58 target-audio hours before conservative exclusions);
an audited packed text-resolution sidecar excluded or corrected suspect
short-clip transcripts without changing source audio. Reference audio was
cropped at 14.96 seconds; about 13.85% of eligible frozen pairs had a
reference shorter than the preferred five seconds, and those exceptions
were kept and counted rather than misreported as long references. The
training data remained packed in Parquet/TAR containers, not millions of
small files.

The deterministic prompt mixture was approximately **55% bare SCRIPT with
local cues**, **20% `GENERAL:` + `SCRIPT:`**, **20% `CAPTION:` + `TRANSCRIPT:`
from available Timbre Whisper or Bude Whisper 1.1 captions**, and **5%
`TRANSCRIPT:` only**. Captions were never fabricated for unannotated UIDs.
The exact renderer and target-text repair code live in `training/`. The
optimizer was AdamW on semantic attention LoRA matrices only, global batch
128 over 32 GH200 GPUs, 5% warm-up, peak LR `2e-5`, one cosine decay to
`2e-6`, gradient clipping at 1, and 26,774 completed steps. This was one
continuous schedule even though Slurm resumed after a code-path repair.
The final resume checkpoint contains the optimizer moments, but a *new*
training dataset requires rebuilding the manifest and changing the
site-specific paths/contracts; do not simply replay the old cursor.

The source worklist and text-resolution sidecar are not embedded in this
model repository. The public core ladder is documented at
[laion/tts-scaling-ladder-de-en](https://huggingface.co/datasets/laion/tts-scaling-ladder-de-en).
Check data licenses and regenerate the exact reference pairing and correction
sidecars before claiming a reproduction. To continue **the same** JUPITER
run, use the `resume_checkpoint.pt` state with the original manifest hash,
same 32-GPU world size, seed, renderer and source-shard order. To adapt to
new data, initialize from `adapter_model.pt` and start a new optimizer and
schedule unless a deliberate migration is implemented.

## What the paired evaluation actually found

A deterministic 24-utterance S3 validation panel (12 German, 12 English)
compared the same prompts, seeds and 5–15-second references with vanilla S3
and this final adapter. The UIDs were held out of this adapter training, but
**speakers were not held out**. On the SCRIPT-only correct-reference setting:

| Metric | Vanilla S3 | This LoRA | Direction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Orange 128-D cosine to the **supplied reference** | 0.746 | 0.711 | Lower with LoRA |
| Orange cosine to the **independent target** | 0.636 | 0.727 | Higher with LoRA |
| Whisper-large-v3-turbo corpus WER | 9.12% | 7.96% | Lower with LoRA |
| Parakeet-v3 corpus WER | 6.14% | 7.63% | Higher with LoRA |

The two ASR instruments disagree; paired bootstrap intervals for both WER
differences include zero. A wrong-speaker-reference swap gave a *smaller*
correct-vs-wrong response with the LoRA (0.513 versus 0.617 for vanilla).
The panel contains weak same-indexed-speaker reference/target pairs: in the
predeclared subset with target/reference cosine at least 0.75 (11 items),
reference cosine rises 0.826 → 0.842, but this small subset is exploratory.
**Do not claim this adapter reliably improves zero-shot cloning, naturalness
or intelligibility.** Listen and test on a larger, truly speaker-disjoint
panel. Orange and ASR are automated proxies, not human listening scores.

The original local listening grid includes reference, original target,
vanilla and LoRA for each of the 24 examples. Its Base64 MP3 audio was not
republished with this model card because the underlying evaluation clips
have separate data-provenance constraints. `evaluation_summary.json` gives
the aggregate numeric record.

# Chatterbox Igbo (NaijaVoices 8-Epoch Fine-Tune)

This repository provides fine-tuned weights for the **ResembleAI Chatterbox T3 Multilingual TTS** model, fine-tuned on **Igbo (`ig`)** speech from the NaijaVoices dataset.

The model extends Chatterbox's autoregressive flow-matching capabilities to Igbo, maintaining strong voice cloning fidelity, natural conversational prosody, and cross-lingual transfer from a reference audio clip.

---

## Model Summary

- **Base Architecture**: Chatterbox T3 (Autoregressive Encodec TTS)
- **Parameters**: ~1.2B
- **Target Language**: Igbo (`ig`)
- **Dataset**: `naijavoices/naijavoices-dataset` (Igbo split)
- **Training Samples**: 8,000 paired audio-text samples
- **Epochs**: 8 full epochs (31,360 total optimization steps)
- **Hardware**: NVIDIA A10G (24 GB VRAM)

---

## Training Convergence & Metrics

The model trained steadily across all 8 epochs with AdamW (learning rate = 5e-5, gradient accumulation steps = 4). Language tokens were initialized by transplanting the `[sw]` (Swahili) donor weights to jumpstart convergence for `ig`.

| 2 | 7840 | 1.1013 | 4.8221 | 5.9234 |

## How to Use

The weights in this repository are **merged** (alpha=0.7) with the base Chatterbox model. 

```bash
git clone https://github.com/resemble-ai/chatterbox.git
cd chatterbox
pip install -e .
```

```python
import torch
import torchaudio
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download, hf_hub_download
from chatterbox.mtl_tts import ChatterboxMultilingualTTS, SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES
from safetensors.torch import load_file
import soundfile as sf
import os

# 1. Add support for our target languages
SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES.update({"yo": "yo", "ig": "ig", "ha": "ha"})
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

# 2. Initialize Base Chatterbox
model = ChatterboxMultilingualTTS.from_pretrained(device)

# 3. Download the merged safetensors from this repo
model_path = hf_hub_download(repo_id="samuelolubukun/chatterbox-igbo-naijavoices", filename="model.safetensors")

# 4. Load the weights directly into the T3 module
sd = load_file(model_path)

import torch.nn as nn
# Manually resize the text embedding and head to match fine-tuned vocab size
old_emb = model.t3.text_emb
model.t3.text_emb = nn.Embedding(sd["text_emb.weight"].shape[0], old_emb.embedding_dim)
old_head = model.t3.text_head
model.t3.text_head = nn.Linear(old_head.in_features, sd["text_head.weight"].shape[0], bias=old_head.bias is not None)

model.t3.load_state_dict(sd, strict=False)
model.t3.to(device).eval()

# 5. Synthesize voice cloning from a reference audio clip
reference_audio = "path/to/reference.wav"
text = "mbize kwesiri ka e lebàra ya anya mgwamgwa ugbua"

# Pad text with a period to help the EOS token trigger properly
text_padded = text.strip() + "." if not text.strip().endswith(".") else text.strip()

with torch.inference_mode():
    out_wav = model.generate(
        text_padded,
        language_id="ig",
        audio_prompt_path=reference_audio,
        exaggeration=1.0,
        cfg_weight=1.0,
        temperature=0.6,
    )

import librosa
import soundfile as sf
audio_np = out_wav.squeeze().cpu().numpy()

# Aggressively trim leading and trailing silence/noise
trimmed_audio, _ = librosa.effects.trim(audio_np, top_db=45)

sf.write("output.wav", trimmed_audio, model.sr)
print("Saved synthesized speech to output.wav")
```

## Limitations and Ethical Usage

- **Domain & Register Bias**: Trained on conversational datasets. Natural prosody transfer depends heavily on the reference clip.
- **Ethical Voice Cloning**: This model is intended for research, linguistic preservation, and accessibility in African languages. Explicit consent should be obtained prior to cloning recognizable individual voices.
